content_voiceover: This table compares the pharmacologic properties of warfarin against the four major DOACs, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban. Warfarin targets VKORC1, has essentially 100% bioavailability, is dosed once daily, but takes four to five days to reach peak effect and has a long 40 hour half-life with no renal clearance. In contrast, the DOACs act quickly, reaching peak effect within one to four hours, and have much shorter half-lives, generally in the range of five to seventeen hours. Dabigatran is notable as the only prodrug among them and has the lowest bioavailability at just 7%, but also the highest renal clearance at 80%, which matters greatly in renal impairment. None of the DOACs require routine monitoring, unlike warfarin which requires INR checks. For drug interactions, warfarin interacts with multiple pathways, while the DOACs mainly interact through P-glycoprotein, and rivaroxaban and apixaban additionally through CYP3A4. Also note the footnotes, warfarin requires overlapping with parenteral anticoagulation when treating VTE, while dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban all require five to ten days of initial parenteral anticoagulation coverage when treating VTE.
keypoints: Warfarin needs 4-5 days to peak; DOACs peak in 1-4 hours
Dabigatran is the only prodrug, with lowest bioavailability at 7%
Dabigatran has highest renal clearance at 80%, a key consideration in renal disease
DOACs need no routine monitoring, unlike warfarin's INR
keypoint_voiceover: Key takeaways. Warfarin needs four to five days to reach peak effect, while DOACs peak within one to four hours. Dabigatran is unique as the only prodrug and has the lowest bioavailability, at just seven percent. Dabigatran also has the highest renal clearance, at 80%, which is critical in patients with renal impairment. And unlike warfarin, none of the DOACs require routine monitoring.
